To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the fatty acid composition of milk, meat and eggs is determined to a great extent by the diet of the livestock, and that this is an area where the food industry can have a significant influence on the fatty acid profile of the final product.

(1) the fatty acid profile of animal-derived foods can be manipulated by altering livestock feeding; (2) the relative proportion of n-3 fatty acid in milk, meat and eggs can be enhanced by increasing the proportion of PUFA-rich feed in animal diets, especially by including fish oil, but the overall PUFA content of these foods remains low; (3) the n-3/n-6 PUFA ratio can be increased in milk and eggs but not in meat;
the fatty acid composition of milk, meat and eggs can be manipulated to provide consumers with more health-benefiting fatty acids by changing the dietary fat source of the livestock.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a sustainable livestock production system which will provide consumers with foods that are not only nutritious but which will also help to prevent the development of chronic disease.
the manipulation of the fatty acid composition of milk, meat and eggs, and the implications for human health.
the manipulation of the fatty acid profile of milk, meat and egg yolk by dietary manipulation of the animal feed to produce foods that are high in n-3 fatty acid, CLA and other bioactive components.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we need to eat less animal-derived food but, if we are going to consume them, we should choose the ones with the highest PUFA content, and that is the ones from animals fed on grass and/or high PUFA oilseeds.

we should be eating less meat, especially from ruminant livestock, and more fish, especially oily fish, but that we should not necessarily be eating less dairy products, especially from grass-fed cattle.
we need to be careful about the type of animal-derived food we choose and the amount we consume.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fatty acid content of milk, eggs and meat is not as important a determinant of dietary intake of long-chain n- 3 PUFA as the amount consumed.
it is possible to increase the content of long-chain n- 3 fatty acids in animal products and this can be achieved without the need for genetic manipulation.
it is possible to manipulate the fat composition in milk, meat and eggs to be more conducive to human health.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a great opportunity for consumers to benefit from the nutritional properties of animal-derived foods if they are willing to pay a premium for these products.
the composition of fatty acids in milk, meat and eggs can be manipulated by the use of specific feeds and feeding regimes.
we should not assume that animal-derived foods are necessarily high in SFA.
